claim: Tunicamycin at 5 µg/ml induces maximal XBP1 mRNA splicing in HeLa cells.
source: At this high concentration, a full-blown UPR was triggered, as is evident from the maximal extent of XBP1 mRNA splicing in HeLa cells, that is, the appearance of a band of higher mobility, corresponding to the RT-PCR product of the XBP1S transcript from which the intron has been removed (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating XBP1 mRNA splicing patterns at different tunicamycin concentrations.

claim: Treatment with 5 µg/ml tunicamycin results in no cell survival after 7 days.
source: Yet, there was no cell survival after 7 days (Figure 1B), not even when the cells were treated with Tm only on the first day for 4 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth/colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tunicamycin at 50 ng/ml induces submaximal XBP1 mRNA splicing transiently.
source: At a 100-fold dilution of the 'standard' concentration, Tm induced the splicing of XBP1 mRNA to submaximal levels, and only transiently so (Figure 1A), but still provoked a substantial cell growth defect (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing XBP1 mRNA splicing patterns at 50 ng/ml tunicamycin in Figure 1A.

claim: Tunicamycin at 25 ng/ml does not induce detectable XBP1 mRNA splicing but still causes some loss of cell growth.
source: Even at a further two-fold dilution of Tm to 25 ng/ml, when no XBP1 mRNA splicing was detected (Figure 1A), there was some loss of cell growth (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from XBP1 splicing assays and cell growth assays shown in Figures 1A, 1B, and 1C.

claim: Deletion of IRE1α and silencing of PERK and ATF6α does not substantially impair cell growth in the absence of tunicamycin.
source: Strikingly, upon deletion of IRE1α by CRISPR/Cas9 and concomitant ablation of PERK and ATF6α by siRNA-mediated silencing (with good efficiency; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), cell growth was hardly impaired.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth assay data and is referenced to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for confirmation of knockdown efficiency.

claim: Cells lacking functional UPR show increased sensitivity to tunicamycin-induced cytotoxicity at lower concentrations.
source: The cytotoxic effects of Tm, however, became apparent in these cells at even lower concentrations than in cells with a functional UPR (Figure 1D), which implies not only that the UPR is predominantly cyto-protective but also that UPR-mediated pro-apoptotic pathways cannot play a decisive role in cell fate upon Tm-driven ER stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth assay data comparing wild-type and UPR-ablated cells shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The UPR is predominantly cyto-protective.
source: The cytotoxic effects of Tm, however, became apparent in these cells at even lower concentrations than in cells with a functional UPR (Figure 1D), which implies not only that the UPR is predominantly cyto-protective but also that UPR-mediated pro-apoptotic pathways cannot play a decisive role in cell fate upon Tm-driven ER stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cells lacking UPR are more sensitive to tunicamycin, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: UPR-mediated pro-apoptotic pathways do not play a decisive role in cell fate upon tunicamycin-driven ER stress.
source: The cytotoxic effects of Tm, however, became apparent in these cells at even lower concentrations than in cells with a functional UPR (Figure 1D), which implies not only that the UPR is predominantly cyto-protective but also that UPR-mediated pro-apoptotic pathways cannot play a decisive role in cell fate upon Tm-driven ER stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that UPR ablation increases sensitivity to tunicamycin, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ER stress-eliciting drugs have pleiotropic effects that obscure how ER homeostatic readjustment can be achieved.
source: Thus, the use of ER stress-eliciting drugs inevitably obscures how ER homeostatic readjustment can be achieved.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tunicamycin causes cytotoxicity independent of UPR activation levels.

claim: Expression of µs in HeLa-µs cells is undetectable in the absence of mifepristone.
source: Expression of µs in HeLa-µs cells in the absence of Mif was undetectable by immunoblotting (Figure 2A) or immunofluorescence (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Different HeLa-µs clones express µs at different levels upon induction with mifepristone.
source: A proxy for tunable expression of µs was offered instead by comparing different HeLa-µs clones, which—due to differences in genomic locus or copy number of integrations—each expressed µs at a different level upon induction with Mif, as shown for three individual clones (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing different µs expression levels in three clones (Hi, Me, Lo) in Figure 2A.

claim: µs expression is uniform among cells within a clone.
source: As illustrated by immunofluorescence of µs (Figure 2B), expression was remarkably uniform among cells because they were clonal.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: µs is retained in the ER lumen.
source: Moreover, µs is retained in the ER lumen, as shown by its strict co-localization with the ER marker CRT (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-localization data with calreticulin shown in Figure 2C.

claim: µs expression in HeLa-µs cells triggers splicing of XBP1 mRNA comparable to tunicamycin treatment.
source: Upon 16 hr of induction of µs expression, splicing of XBP1 mRNA, phosphorylation of PERK (appearance of a band of slightly lower mobility), expression of PERK's downstream effector CHOP, cleavage of the precursor ATF6α-p90 and the concomitant release of its cytosolic portion p50 were all at levels comparable to those triggered by a conventional Tm- or Tg-elicited UPR in these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing XBP1 mRNA splicing in Figure 2A.

claim: µs expression triggers phosphorylation of PERK comparable to tunicamycin treatment.
source: Upon 16 hr of induction of µs expression, splicing of XBP1 mRNA, phosphorylation of PERK (appearance of a band of slightly lower mobility), expression of PERK's downstream effector CHOP, cleavage of the precursor ATF6α-p90 and the concomitant release of its cytosolic portion p50 were all at levels comparable to those triggered by a conventional Tm- or Tg-elicited UPR in these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing PERK phosphorylation in Figure 2A.

claim: µs expression triggers CHOP expression comparable to tunicamycin treatment.
source: Upon 16 hr of induction of µs expression, splicing of XBP1 mRNA, phosphorylation of PERK (appearance of a band of slightly lower mobility), expression of PERK's downstream effector CHOP, cleavage of the precursor ATF6α-p90 and the concomitant release of its cytosolic portion p50 were all at levels comparable to those triggered by a conventional Tm- or Tg-elicited UPR in these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing CHOP levels in Figure 2A.

claim: µs expression triggers cleavage of ATF6α-p90 and release of p50 comparable to thapsigargin treatment.
source: Upon 16 hr of induction of µs expression, splicing of XBP1 mRNA, phosphorylation of PERK (appearance of a band of slightly lower mobility), expression of PERK's downstream effector CHOP, cleavage of the precursor ATF6α-p90 and the concomitant release of its cytosolic portion p50 were all at levels comparable to those triggered by a conventional Tm- or Tg-elicited UPR in these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing ATF6α cleavage in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment of HeLa-MifON cells with mifepristone does not provoke XBP1 mRNA splicing.
source: Treatment of the parental HeLa-MifON cells with a high dose of Mif (10 nM) did not provoke XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: UPR activation in mifepristone-treated HeLa-µs cells is the result of µs expression.
source: Thus, the UPR induction in Mif-treated HeLa-µs was the result of µs expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mifepristone alone does not induce UPR in parental cells (Figure 2G), but does in HeLa-µs cells (Figure 2A).

claim: UPR activation upon µs induction is dose-dependent.
source: Moreover, UPR activation upon µs induction was dose-dependent, as the extent of XBP1 mRNA splicing or CHOP expression was commensurate with the levels of µs that were expressed by the different HeLa-µs clones (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing UPR markers across different clones expressing different levels of µs in Figure 2A.

claim: IRE1α clusters upon µs expression.
source: With doxycycline (Dox), we tuned IRE1α-GFP expression to near-endogenous levels that allowed visualization by fluorescent microscopy and found that IRE1α-GFP clustered not only upon Tm treatment but also upon µs expression (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing IRE1α-GFP clustering in Figure 2H.

claim: µs expression drives activation of all three UPR branches in a similar manner and extent as ER stress-eliciting drugs.
source: Altogether, we concluded that µs expression drove the activation of all branches of the UPR that we tested, in a similar manner and to a similar extent as when they were triggered by ER stress-eliciting drugs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations comparing µs-induced UPR to drug-induced UPR (Figures 2A, 2H).

claim: Cell growth of HeLa-µs cells expressing µs almost parallels that of mifepristone-treated parental MifON cells.
source: Strikingly, in spite of the expression of µs in bulk, the cell growth of the HeLa-µs cells almost paralleled that of the Mif-treated parental MifON cells (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The full-blown UPR elicited by µs expression is well tolerated by cells.
source: Thus, the full-blown UPR that was elicited by µs expression was well tolerated by the cells, unlike prolonged treatment with Tm at concentrations that triggered a full-blown UPR (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing cell growth data from µs-expressing cells (Figure 2I,J) with tunicamycin-treated cells (Figure 1).

claim: HeLa-µs cells offer a suitable model to assess ER homeostatic readjustment and the role of the UPR.
source: In all, we concluded that the HeLa-µs cells offer a suitable model to assess ER homeostatic readjustment and the role of the UPR in this process, as the cells apparently cope well with the proteostatic insult that is unabated once µs expression is induced.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that cells tolerate µs expression well and undergo successful homeostatic readjustment.

claim: Co-expression of λ and µs in excess λ allows successful assembly into polymeric antibodies that are efficiently secreted.
source: The clone in which λ was in excess allowed successful assembly into polymeric antibodies that were efficiently secreted.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing IgM assembly and secretion patterns in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: In clones where µs is in excess over λ, IgM assembly and secretion are less efficient, leading to intracellular accumulation of disulfide-linked intermediates.
source: In clones where µs was in excess, assembly and secretion were less efficient, leading to intracellular accumulation of disulfide-linked species that are characteristic intermediates of the IgM assembly pathway (Hendershot and Sitia, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing assembly intermediates in Figure 3B and is also supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HeLa cells inducibly expressing λ at high levels do not activate the UPR.
source: As anticipated, HeLa cells inducibly expressing λ—at similarly high levels as reached for µs—did not activate the UPR (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing lack of UPR markers in λ-expressing cells in Figure 3C.

claim: The µs-provoked UPR is almost fully mitigated when λ is co-expressed in excess.
source: Strikingly, the µs-provoked UPR was also almost fully mitigated when λ was co-expressed in excess, while the other clones showed intermediate UPR activation commensurate with an excess of µs (or lack of λ).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing UPR markers in different µs+λ clones in Figure 3C.

claim: The flux of proteins entering the ER is not a key determinant for UPR activation.
source: As the levels of ER client proteins (the sum of intracellular λ and µs) were comparable in the different clones, we concluded that the flux of proteins entering the ER is no key determinant for UPR activation, but rather that the nature of the proteostatic insult determines the extent of UPR activation, with λ being a very poor UPR activator, and µs being a particularly powerful one, provided it does not team up with λ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing UPR activation across clones with similar total client protein levels but different λ:µs ratios (Figure 3).

claim: The nature of the proteostatic insult determines the extent of UPR activation.
source: As the levels of ER client proteins (the sum of intracellular λ and µs) were comparable in the different clones, we concluded that the flux of proteins entering the ER is no key determinant for UPR activation, but rather that the nature of the proteostatic insult determines the extent of UPR activation, with λ being a very poor UPR activator, and µs being a particularly powerful one, provided it does not team up with λ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing UPR activation in cells expressing different combinations of λ and µs (Figure 3).

claim: λ is a very poor UPR activator.
source: As the levels of ER client proteins (the sum of intracellular λ and µs) were comparable in the different clones, we concluded that the flux of proteins entering the ER is no key determinant for UPR activation, but rather that the nature of the proteostatic insult determines the extent of UPR activation, with λ being a very poor UPR activator, and µs being a particularly powerful one, provided it does not team up with λ.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing minimal UPR activation in λ-expressing cells (Figure 3C).

claim: µs is a particularly powerful UPR activator when not paired with λ.
source: As the levels of ER client proteins (the sum of intracellular λ and µs) were comparable in the different clones, we concluded that the flux of proteins entering the ER is no key determinant for UPR activation, but rather that the nature of the proteostatic insult determines the extent of UPR activation, with λ being a very poor UPR activator, and µs being a particularly powerful one, provided it does not team up with λ.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing strong UPR activation in µs-only expressing cells (Figure 2A) and reduced activation when λ is present (Figure 3C).

claim: BiP levels increase markedly when µs is expressed alone but far less or not at all if λ is present.
source: Of note is that levels of BiP increased markedly when µs was expressed alone but far less so or not at all if λ was present (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and quantification data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: BiP binds to µs until it is displaced by λ.
source: Indeed, it has been established in plasma cells that BiP binds to µs until it is displaced by λ (Bole et al., 1986; Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bole et al., 1986) and illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: BiP levels increase approximately 12.5-fold upon µs expression.
source: BiP levels increased ~12.5 fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunoblotting data using BiP standards (Figure 4B).

claim: BiP levels rise from approximately 2×10^7 to approximately 2×10^8 copies per cell upon µs expression.
source: On the basis of cell counting, determination of the protein weight of the samples and the known molecular weight of BiP of ~70 kDa, we estimated that BiP levels rise from ~2×107 to ~2×108 copies per cell.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from quantitative immunoblotting data, cell counting, and protein weight measurements.

claim: BiP levels are in excess of µs once cells have adapted to the proteostatic insult.
source: Importantly, from the absolute quantitation, we deduced that BiP levels were in excess of µs once the cells had adapted to the proteostatic insult (with µs reaching an estimated ~1.5–1.8×108 copies per cell).
evidence: The claim is inferred from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Early upon onset of µs expression, µs levels are transiently at 1:1 stoichiometry with BiP or possibly exceed BiP levels.
source: Early upon the onset of µs expression and before BiP induction was fully underway, however, µs levels were transiently at a 1:1 stoichiometry with those of BiP, or possibly, µs levels even slightly exceeded BiP levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All three UPR branches transiently reach maximal output upon onset of µs expression.
source: Following the activation of the UPR over time upon onset of µs expression, we found that all three UPR branches transiently reached an output that was maximal, that is at least on a par with the output that was induced by a conventional drug-elicited UPR (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data of UPR markers shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: Levels of cleaved ATF6α (p50) reach a maximum at approximately 6 hours after onset of µs expression.
source: Levels of cleaved ATF6α (p50) reached a maximum at ~6 hr after the onset of µs expression before it subsided to submaximal levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Full-length ATF6α (p90) is largely depleted after the initial burst of p50 release.
source: The full-length precursor ATF6α (p90) was in large part depleted after this intial burst of ATF6α (p50) release (Figure 4C), such that the determining factor for the amplitude of signaling through the ATF6α branch was inevitably, the de novo synthesis of p90 rather than the severity of the proteostatic insult, at least for a while before levels of p90 were fully restored.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data showing ATF6α p90 and p50 levels over time in Figure 4C.

claim: Levels of spliced XBP1 mRNA reach a maximum at approximately 6 hours of µs expression and remain maximal for about 24 hours.
source: Levels of spliced XBP1 mRNA likewise reached a maximum at ~6 hr of µs expression, and remained maximal for about 24 hr (with perhaps some oscillations) before they subsided to submaximal levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CHOP levels reach a maximum at 12-16 hours after onset of µs expression.
source: Levels of CHOP, which provides a readout for PERK activity, reached a maximum slightly later, at 12–16 hr after the onset of µs expression, before reaching submaximal levels, as further illustrated in a 'heatmap' of UPR activation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with ER stress-eliciting drugs during chronic µs expression readily triggers close to maximal UPR output.
source: Treatment with ER stress-eliciting drugs during the chronic phase when the UPR had submaximal output readily triggered close to maximal output of all three UPR branches (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), indicating that prolonged µs expression had not exhausted the signaling capacity of the UPR, and thus, that homeostatic readjustment of the ER accounted for lowered UPR output levels upon chronic µs expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Prolonged µs expression does not exhaust the signaling capacity of the UPR.
source: Treatment with ER stress-eliciting drugs during the chronic phase when the UPR had submaximal output readily triggered close to maximal output of all three UPR branches (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), indicating that prolonged µs expression had not exhausted the signaling capacity of the UPR, and thus, that homeostatic readjustment of the ER accounted for lowered UPR output levels upon chronic µs expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cells with chronic µs expression can still mount a full UPR response to drugs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: Homeostatic readjustment of the ER accounts for lowered UPR output levels upon chronic µs expression.
source: Treatment with ER stress-eliciting drugs during the chronic phase when the UPR had submaximal output readily triggered close to maximal output of all three UPR branches (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), indicating that prolonged µs expression had not exhausted the signaling capacity of the UPR, and thus, that homeostatic readjustment of the ER accounted for lowered UPR output levels upon chronic µs expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that UPR capacity is not exhausted during chronic µs expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: The highest UPR output coincides with the highest µs/BiP ratio.
source: Strikingly, the highest output of the three UPR branches did not coincide with µs having reached maximal expression levels. Instead, UPR signaling reached maxima when the ratio µs/BiP was highest (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing temporal patterns of µs/BiP ratios (Figure 4B) with UPR activation levels (Figure 4D).

claim: UPR signals are commensurate with the extent to which BiP is sequestered by µs rather than by µs accumulation per se.
source: These findings support a scenario in which the UPR signals are commensurate with the extent to which the folding machinery, in particular BiP, is sequested by µs rather than by µs accumulation per se.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that maximal UPR activation correlates with the µs/BiP ratio rather than absolute µs levels (Figures 4B, 4D).

claim: Before induction of µs expression, the ER lumen occupies 10-12% of the cytoplasmic area in electron micrographs.
source: We determined that, before induction of µs expression, the ER lumen occupies 10–12% of the area within the cytoplasm (i.e. excluding the nucleus) in the electron micrographs (Figure 5), which by a rough estimate would correspond to (0.10–0.12)3/2≈3–4% of the cytoplasmic volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ER has an estimated volume of approximately 60-80 fl before µs expression.
source: Considering that the volume of the cytosol in HeLa cells is estimated to be ~2×103 µm3, that is ~2×103 fl (Milo, 2013), we estimated the ER to have a volume of ~60–80 fl.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from EM measurements and cited literature values for cytosolic volume (Milo, 2013).

claim: The ER expands to cover approximately 18% of cytoplasmic area within 1-3 days of µs expression.
source: The ER expanded in the course of 1–3 days upon the onset of µs expression to cover ~18% of the cytoplasmic area in the electron micrographs, corresponding to roughly (0.18)3/2≈7–8% of the cytoplasmic volume, but we observed no further ER expansion after 3 days.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The volume of the ER increases 2-3-fold upon µs expression to approximately 120-240 fl per cell.
source: On the basis of these estimates, the volume of the ER increased 2–3-fold as a result of µs expression, to ~120–240 fl per cell.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ER accounts for approximately 3% of total protein content before µs expression.
source: We then calculated the percentage of the total protein for each category and deduced that the ER accounts for ~3% of total protein content before µs expression in line with the findings by EM.
evidence: The claim is supported by label-free quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Upon µs expression, the ER content expands to approximately 10% of total protein within 3 days.
source: Upon µs expression, the ER content, including µs, expanded to ~10% within 3 days, but did not expand much further after that (~12% at day 7) (Figure 6, upper panels; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by label-free quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BiP levels increase approximately 8-fold between day 0 and day 7 of µs expression according to label-free quantitation.
source: Most notably, between day 0 and 7, levels of BiP increased ~8-fold (and ~14-fold according to SILAC measurements; Supplementary file 1), in good agreement with the absolute quantitations we obtained by immunoblotting (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by label-free quantitative proteomics data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: BiP levels increase approximately 14-fold between day 0 and day 7 of µs expression according to SILAC measurements.
source: Most notably, between day 0 and 7, levels of BiP increased ~8-fold (and ~14-fold according to SILAC measurements; Supplementary file 1), in good agreement with the absolute quantitations we obtained by immunoblotting (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: At day 7 of µs expression, BiP becomes the second most abundant protein in cells after β-actin.
source: In fact, at day 7, BiP became the second most abundant protein in the cells (after β-actin), amounting to ~4% of the total proteome mass.
evidence: The claim is supported by label-free quantitative proteomics data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Cells harbor an average of 5 × 10^9 proteins.
source: Put together with the absolute quantitation of BiP levels, we estimate that the cells harbor an average of 5 × 109 proteins, which fits with earlier assumptions (Milo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from BiP quantitation data and is consistent with cited literature (Milo, 2013).

claim: BiP concentration is approximately 0.5 mM before induction of µs expression.
source: Moreover, from these quantitations, we estimated BiP levels to be at ~0.5 mM (or 30–40 mg/ml) before induction and to reach ~1.5 mM (or 90–120 mg/ml) in the ~3-fold expanded ER at day 7, accounting for about a third of the estimated ~200–300 mg/ml overall protein concentration in the lumen of the organelle.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from BiP quantitation and ER volume measurements.

claim: BiP concentration reaches approximately 1.5 mM in the expanded ER at day 7 of µs expression.
source: Moreover, from these quantitations, we estimated BiP levels to be at ~0.5 mM (or 30–40 mg/ml) before induction and to reach ~1.5 mM (or 90–120 mg/ml) in the ~3-fold expanded ER at day 7, accounting for about a third of the estimated ~200–300 mg/ml overall protein concentration in the lumen of the organelle.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from BiP quantitation and ER volume measurements.

claim: BiP accounts for about a third of the estimated 200-300 mg/ml overall protein concentration in the ER lumen at day 7.
source: Moreover, from these quantitations, we estimated BiP levels to be at ~0.5 mM (or 30–40 mg/ml) before induction and to reach ~1.5 mM (or 90–120 mg/ml) in the ~3-fold expanded ER at day 7, accounting for about a third of the estimated ~200–300 mg/ml overall protein concentration in the lumen of the organelle.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from BiP quantitation and ER volume measurements.

claim: BiP levels within the ER increase from approximately 15% before µs expression to 30-40% of the expanded ER proteome.
source: As a consequence, levels of BiP within the ER increased from ~15% before the onset of µs expression to 30–40% of the expanded ER proteome.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: ERdj co-chaperones of BiP are upregulated upon µs expression but to levels about two orders of magnitude lower than BiP levels.
source: The ERdj co-chaperones of BiP were upregulated upon µs expression as well, but, surprisingly perhaps, to levels that were still about two orders of magnitude lower than the levels of BiP itself (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: ERdj co-chaperones execute their function in a sub-stoichiometric fashion in the HeLa-µs model.
source: Thus, their co-chaperone function must be executed in a sub-stoichiometric fashion in the HeLa-µs model.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ERdj levels are much lower than BiP levels (Supplementary file 1).

claim: µs levels rapidly increase to become approximately 1% of total protein content after 1 day of expression.
source: Before induction, µs was barely detectable (~1 ppm) but levels rapidly increased to become ~10×103 ppm, that is ~1% (after 1 day) and ~2% (from day 3 onward) of the total protein content in the cell (Figure 6, upper panels; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: After 1 day of µs expression, µs levels exceed those of any ER chaperone except BiP.
source: Strikingly, 1 day of expression was sufficient for µs levels to exceed that of any chaperone in the ER except those of BiP, which still outmatched µs 3:2 (Figure 6, lower panels; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BiP levels increase 3-4-fold during the first day of µs expression.
source: Yet, BiP levels had increased 3–4-fold during that first day to keep pace with the burden imposed on the ER folding machinery by µs.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BiP and µs together constitute about half of the ER protein mass when the ER has fully expanded.
source: At later times, the margin by which BiP levels were in excess of µs levels increased again, with BiP and µs together constituting about half of the ER protein mass when it had fully expanded.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Upon µs expression in bulk, the ER undergoes approximately 3-4-fold expansion.
source: Thus, upon µs expression in bulk, the ER content not only changed quantitatively (i.e. undergoing a ~ 3–4-fold expansion), but also qualitatively (i.e. becoming dominated by µs that is held in check by excess levels of its most devoted chaperone BiP).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy and proteomics data (Figures 5, 6).

claim: Upon µs expression, the ER becomes dominated by µs held in check by excess BiP.
source: Thus, upon µs expression in bulk, the ER content not only changed quantitatively (i.e. undergoing a ~ 3–4-fold expansion), but also qualitatively (i.e. becoming dominated by µs that is held in check by excess levels of its most devoted chaperone BiP).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing BiP and µs dominate the ER proteome (Figure 6).

claim: Ablation of all three UPR branches does not substantially impede cell growth in HeLa-µs cells in the absence of µs expression.
source: As we have shown above for wild-type HeLa cells (Figure 1D) ablation of all three UPR branches together hardly impeded cell growth in HeLa-µs cells in the absence of µs expression (Figure 7A,B), probably because HeLa cells by default handle a low secretory load (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Expression of µs in cells with all UPR branches ablated fully abolishes cell growth.
source: Concomitant expression of µs, however, fully abolished cell growth (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: µs expression causes synthetic lethality when all UPR branches are ablated.
source: Annexin V staining confirmed that µs expression caused synthetic lethality under conditions when all UPR branches were ablated (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The UPR is essential for ER homeostatic readjustment upon µs expression.
source: Thus, we concluded that the UPR is essential for ER homeostatic readjustment upon µs expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cells lacking UPR cannot survive µs expression (Figures 7A-C).

claim: ER expansion is not necessarily provoked by bulk synthesis of client proteins per se.
source: Interestingly, ER expansion is not necessarily provoked by bulk synthesis of client proteins per se, as co-expression of sufficient quantities of λ led to bulk secretion of IgM but failed to trigger a strong UPR, and, thus, did not result in augmented BiP production (which served as a proxy for ER expansion).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that λ+µs co-expression with excess λ does not trigger strong UPR or BiP upregulation (Figure 3).

claim: The ER folding machinery is underused in HeLa cells.
source: Our findings indicate moreover that the ER folding machinery seems to be underused in HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that λ expression does not trigger UPR and that HeLa cells have low secretory load (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1).

claim: Mobilization of the default ER folding machinery is sufficient for productive folding and assembly of IgM from stoichiometrically expressed subunits.
source: Apparently, mobilization of the default ER folding machinery is sufficient for a task that can be productively executed, such as the folding and assembly of IgM from subunits that are expressed in bulk but in the correct stoichiometry.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that λ+µs co-expression with excess λ allows efficient IgM assembly without strong UPR activation (Figure 3).

claim: A substantial fraction of BiP is kept in reserve in an inactive, AMPylated form under non-ER stress conditions.
source: In line with such a notion, a substantial fraction of BiP is kept in reserve in an inactive, AMPylated form under non-ER stress conditions (Preissler et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Preissler et al., 2015).

claim: BiP binding to µs must be highly stringent out of immunological necessity.
source: Thus, BiP binding to µs must be highly stringent out of immunological necessity (Anelli and van Anken, 2013), which correlates with the fact that mutations in µs that lead to lowered affinity for BiP are associated with disorders of the immune system, such as lymphoproliferative heavy chain disease or myeloma (Hendershot et al., 1987; Anelli and Sitia, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anelli and van Anken, 2013; Hendershot et al., 1987; Anelli and Sitia, 2010).

claim: Mutations in µs that lead to lowered affinity for BiP are associated with lymphoproliferative heavy chain disease or myeloma.
source: Thus, BiP binding to µs must be highly stringent out of immunological necessity (Anelli and van Anken, 2013), which correlates with the fact that mutations in µs that lead to lowered affinity for BiP are associated with disorders of the immune system, such as lymphoproliferative heavy chain disease or myeloma (Hendershot et al., 1987; Anelli and Sitia, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hendershot et al., 1987; Anelli and Sitia, 2010).

claim: During B to plasma cell differentiation, all cellular machineries develop in a strict sequential order that allows them to anticipate bulk IgM production.
source: In the course of B to plasma cell differentiation, however, all cellular machineries develop in a strict sequential order that allows them to anticipate bulk IgM production (van Anken et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (van Anken et al., 2003).

claim: The purely µs-driven stimulus results almost exclusively in ER expansion with meager expansion of the remainder of the secretory machinery.
source: Conversely, the purely µs-driven stimulus that we investigated in this study resulted almost exclusively in ER expansion. We found only meager indications of the expansion of even the remainder of the secretory machinery (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Stringent retention of µs in the ER by BiP obviates the need to reinforce the secretory pathway downstream of the ER.
source: One could argue that the stringent retention of µs in the ER by BiP would obviate the need to reinforce the secretory pathway downstream of the ER.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that µs is retained in the ER.

claim: Homeostatic regulation of the Golgi and compartments beyond is governed foremost by dedicated signaling mechanisms distinct from the UPR.
source: Accordingly, homeostatic regulation of the Golgi and compartments beyond appears to be governed foremost by dedicated signaling mechanisms distinct from the UPR (Luini and Parashuraman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Luini and Parashuraman, 2016).

claim: Maximal UPR activation correlates with a shortage of BiP in matching the accumulating load of µs.
source: Importantly, we found that maximal UPR activation correlated with a shortage of BiP in matching the accumulating load of µs, rather than with accumulation of client protein in the ER per se.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing temporal patterns of BiP/µs ratios with UPR activation levels (Figures 4B, 4D).

claim: The UPR transitions to chronic submaximal levels when BiP is in excess again.
source: Indeed, the transitioning of UPR signaling to chronic submaximal levels coincided with the ER becoming dominated by BiP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing temporal patterns of BiP levels with UPR activation levels (Figures 4, 6).

claim: The PiZ mutant of α1-antitrypsin does not sequester BiP and fails to trigger the UPR despite accumulating in the ER.
source: Accordingly, despite its accumulation in the ER, the PiZ mutant of α1-antitrypsin does not sequester BiP and fails to trigger the UPR (Graham et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Graham et al., 1990).

claim: Sequestering of BiP by µs is sufficient to activate IRE1α and PERK in vitro.
source: An in vitro study moreover suggests that sequestering of BiP by µs would be sufficient to activate IRE1α and PERK (Carrara et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Carrara et al., 2015).

claim: Ire1/IRE1α activates through direct binding of unfolded proteins.
source: However, based on the crystal structure of yeast Ire1's lumenal domain (Credle et al., 2005), Peter Walter and colleagues proposed instead that Ire1 activates through direct binding of unfolded proteins, for which in vitro evidence has subsequently been obtained for both yeast Ire1 (Gardner and Walter, 2011) and mammalian IRE1α (Karagöz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Credle et al., 2005; Gardner and Walter, 2011; Karagöz et al., 2017).

claim: The UPR transducers are in the OFF state when bound to BiP and in the ON state when bound to clients.
source: Assuming that the UPR signaling amplitude is commensurate with that of ER stress sensing by the UPR transducers, it is tempting to conclude that the UPR transducers are in the OFF state (as ER stress sensors) when bound to BiP, and in the ON state when bound to clients.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the authors' data and prior models.

claim: In a three-way competition between sensor-BiP, sensor-client, and BiP-client complexes, the ratio between sensor-client and sensor-BiP robustly reports on the ratio between client and BiP.
source: So in a three-way competition between formation of sensor-BiP, sensor-client, and BiP-client complexes, the ratio between sensor-client (ON) and sensor-BiP (OFF) will most robustly report on the ratio between client and BiP.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the authors' model of ratiometric sensing.

claim: The two models for ER stress sensor activation (BiP dissociation and direct client binding) can be reconciled in a model of ratiometric ER stress sensing.
source: Thus, the two models for ER stress sensor activation can be reconciled easily in a model of ratiometric ER stress sensing, in line with our observations that the UPR signaling output is highest when the levels of the ER client µs eclipse those of BiP, and that UPR signaling subsides to submaximal levels when an excess of BiP over the client is restored.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' data showing correlation between BiP/µs ratios and UPR activation (Figures 4B, 4D).

claim: Homeostatic readjustment of the ER entails that the UPR output becomes submaximal.
source: The finding that homeostatic readjustment of the ER entails that the UPR output becomes submaximal is also relevant for disease.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' data showing UPR transitions to submaximal levels during chronic µs expression (Figure 4).

claim: Cells suffering from genetic disorders causing ER client protein misfolding will likely adapt and display submaximal UPR signaling levels.
source: Various genetic disorders stem from mutations in ER client proteins that lead to their misfolding and accumulation in the ER. On the basis of our results, cells that suffer from such conditions will likely adapt and display submaximal UPR signaling levels similar to those that we found for chronic µs expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative extrapolation from the authors' findings to disease contexts.

claim: Submaximal UPR signaling reflects chronic stress rather than mild ER stress.
source: In other words, submaximal UPR signaling is not a sign of 'mild' ER stress, but rather reflects that the stress is chronic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' data showing that chronic µs expression leads to submaximal UPR despite ongoing stress (Figure 4).

claim: The HeLa-µs cell model provides an excellent tool to dissect how the UPR alleviates ER stress and evaluates the success of ER homeostatic readjustment.
source: Finally, since successful ER homeostatic readjustment upon µs-driven proteostatic ER stress critically depends on the UPR, the HeLa-µs cell model provides an excellent tool to dissect in greater detail how the UPR alleviates ER stress, and how it may serve to evaluate the success of ER homeostatic readjustment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' findings that the model allows study of successful ER homeostatic readjustment.

claim: A variety of disorders ranging from cancer to diabetes tie in with aberrant or maladaptive UPR-driven cell fate decisions.
source: The latter aspect is key, because a variety of disorders, ranging from cancer to diabetes, tie in with aberrant or maladaptive UPR-driven cell fate decisions (Wang and Kaufman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wang and Kaufman, 2012).
